did_you_know.text: Did you know? In this chapter, Eliphaz the Temanite responds to Job and continues their debate about the meaning of Job’s suffering and God’s ways.
Did you know? Eliphaz argues that many words of rebuke are useless when they do not strengthen reverence for God and may even be of no benefit.
Did you know? Eliphaz uses rhetorical questions to challenge Job’s sense of uniqueness, asking whether Job was the first human ever born or was present at the creation of the world.
Did you know? Eliphaz appeals to the wisdom of the elders, claiming that even among his listeners there are people older and more experienced than Job.
Did you know? Eliphaz presents human beings as unable to claim absolute purity and righteousness because they are born of woman.

Did you know? Eliphaz extends his argument by saying that even the holy ones and the heavens are not considered completely pure in God’s sight; this is his position in the debate, not a view presented as universally accepted throughout the Book of Job.
Did you know? Eliphaz presents his words as knowledge he is about to share from what he has seen and heard, attributing them to a tradition passed down among the wise from their ancestors.
Did you know? In Eliphaz’s description, the wicked live their entire lives in fear and inner turmoil, even when there is outward peace.
Did you know? Eliphaz describes the wicked person as raising his hand against God and trying to confront Him with thick shields—a picture of rebellion and defiance.

Did you know? At the end of the chapter, Eliphaz warns that those who trust in what is worthless will gain nothing from it, and he describes the wicked person’s end using images of fruit that never ripens, a withering branch, and deceit conceived in the heart.
